title: Taking part in sports competitions: six opinions

script.text: Everybody says our crowd wins matches at home, and it's true that I like it when the stands are full. But last season one home match was played in front of nobody because of the rain, and I still scored twice. I know our pitch: where the ball jumps off the fence, which corner stays muddy. Away, I play like a stranger, and I can't predict a single bounce.

People think a referee is there to catch players out. In fact most of my work happens before the whistle: I explain to both captains how I'll treat a tackle from behind, so that they trust me when it happens. Everyone takes part to win, of course, and a good team will push hard. But once the players stop believing the official is fair, the match is just a fight.

After we lost the semi-final, my coach said that at least I'd taken part, which didn't help at all. I never watch videos after a win, but that evening I watched the whole match three times and counted how many long rallies I'd given away. Eleven. I changed my training, and this spring I beat the same girl in two sets.

I took part in the town marathon as a volunteer, expecting to hand out water and go home. Nobody could predict who would win the women's race, so the whole main street stood and waited. Afterwards people from other cities packed the cafés, my neighbour, who complains about everything, offered a room to two runners from Poland, and the shops did more business than in a normal week.

I've had a season ticket for fifteen years, and I remember almost nothing about the 4–0 games. What I remember is a match we lost 3–2 in the last minute. Nobody in the stadium knew how it would end, so everybody stood and held their breath. My friend only comes when we play the big teams, because he wants to see us win.

In training I'm the fastest in my group, almost a second ahead, and I know every tile of our home pool. Then on the day my arms feel like rubber. My mum says 'Enjoy it', my coach says 'Relax', and I'm thinking about coming last. Last month I was so tense that I left the block too early, and the referee told me my time wouldn't count.

options: Taking part is more important than winning.
A team plays better on its home pitch.
Every competition needs a referee that players trust.
A big race can bring visitors and money to a town.
Nerves on the day can spoil an athlete's result.
Losing a match can teach an athlete a lot.
The best matches are the ones nobody can predict.
discuss: Which of the six speakers do you agree with most, and why?
Speaker C calls a defeat 'a favour'. Have you ever learnt something important from losing?
Is it worth putting up with road closures and crowds when your city hosts a big sporting event?
Would you rather watch a close match between two average teams or a one-sided game with a famous star?
